examples.ko: 이름을 부르자 그가 천천히 뒤돌아서 웃었어요.
examples.en: When I called his name, he slowly turned around and smiled.
Someone called me and I turned around, but nobody was there.
Don't turn around; just look ahead and keep walking.

examples.ko: 선생님이 칠판을 쓰다가 뒤돌아 학생들을 보셨어요.
examples.en: The teacher turned around from writing on the board and looked at the students.

examples.ko: 엄마가 가다가 뒤돌아봐도 아이는 울지 않았어요.
examples.en: Even when Mom looked back while leaving, the child didn't cry.

examples.ko: 저를 보더니 그 사람이 갑자기 뒤돌아요.
examples.en: Seeing me, that person suddenly turns around.

explain: 몸을 돌려 뒤쪽을 향하는 동작이에요. '뒤돌아서다'는 몸 전체를 돌려 서는 느낌이고, '뒤돌아보다'는 뒤를 보는 거예요. '지난날을 뒤돌아보다'처럼 과거를 생각할 때도 써요.

phrases.nuance_en: The action of turning to look behind you.

phrases.en: He turned around without a word.
phrases.nuance_en: Feels like turning your whole body around.

phrases.en: Don't turn around, just look ahead.
phrases.nuance_ko: 하지 말라고 말할 때 쓰는 표현이에요.
phrases.nuance_en: A phrase for telling someone not to do it.

explain_en: It describes turning your body to face backward. '뒤돌아서다' feels like turning your whole body, and '뒤돌아보다' means looking behind. '지난날을 뒤돌아보다' also uses it for reflecting on the past.

examples.ko: 누가 뒤따라오는 것 같아서 돌아보니 제 그림자였어요.
examples.en: I felt someone following me, but when I looked back, it was my shadow.
The puppy keeps following me.

examples.ko: 먼저 가 계세요. 제가 곧 뒤따라올게요.
examples.en: Please go ahead. I'll come along right after you.
The children followed the teacher in a line.

examples.ko: 택시가 우리 차를 계속 뒤따라와서 놀랐어요.
examples.en: I was startled because a taxi kept following our car.
My friend came along ten minutes later.

explain: 말하는 사람이 있는 쪽으로 누군가 뒤에서 따라올 때 써요. 멀어지는 쪽이면 '뒤따라가다'를 써요. '약속 장소에 먼저 가 있을게요, 뒤따라오세요'처럼 나중에 오라고 말할 때도 좋아요.

phrases.nuance_ko: 앞에서 안내하며 따라오라고 할 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used when leading and telling someone to follow.

phrases.en: Please go in first. I'll follow you in.
phrases.nuance_ko: 나중에 그쪽으로 오겠다고 말할 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used to say you will come to that place later.
Shorter than 뒤따라오다 and more common.

explain_en: Use it when someone follows behind toward where the speaker is. If they move away from the speaker, use '뒤따라가다'. It is also handy for telling someone to come later, as in 'I'll be at the meeting spot, please follow after me'.

en: to step aside; to move aside

examples.en: When the ambulance came, the cars moved aside.

examples.ko: 좁은 계단에서는 서로 한쪽으로 비켜서면 돼요.
examples.en: On a narrow staircase, you can both step to one side.
I stepped aside for a moment and then walked on.

examples.ko: 문 옆에 비켜서서 사람들이 내리기를 기다렸어요.
examples.en: I stood aside by the door and waited for people to get off.
I stepped to one side, but I still bumped into someone.

examples.ko: 엘리베이터 앞에서 길을 막지 말고 비켜서야 해요.
examples.en: In front of the elevator, don't block the way; you should step aside.

explain: '비키다'는 길에서 몸이나 물건을 옮겨 자리를 내줄 때 쓰고, '비켜서다'는 비켜서 어느 쪽에 서 있는 모습까지 담아요. 부탁할 때는 '좀 비켜 주세요'라고 해요. '비켜!'는 반말이라 무례하게 들릴 수 있어요.

phrases.en: When a bike comes, I move to the side.
phrases.nuance_ko: 자리를 내주려고 몸이나 물건을 옮기는 동작을 말하고, 서 있는 모습은 담지 않아요.
phrases.nuance_en: Means moving out of the way, without the sense of then standing there.
phrases.en_equiv: to move out of the way

phrases.en: People stepped aside to one side of the road.
phrases.nuance_ko: 어느 쪽으로 비켜서는지 말할 때 '한쪽으로', '옆으로'와 함께 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used with 한쪽으로 or 옆으로 to say which way someone steps aside.
phrases.en_equiv: to step aside to one side

phrases.en: Excuse me, could you please move aside?
phrases.nuance_ko: 길을 비켜 달라고 정중하게 부탁할 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: A polite way to ask someone to let you pass.

explain_en: '비키다' means to move out of the way (a body or an object), while '비켜서다' also suggests standing off to one side. When asking, say '좀 비켜 주세요'. '비켜!' is casual speech and can sound rude.

examples.en: A truck carries the goods to the warehouse.
Workers carried the moving boxes to the new house.
The two of us will carry the heavy box.
A vehicle carrying a patient to the hospital passed by.
After moving the goods, I took a rest.
Please leave the carried luggage in front of the door.

explain: 무거운 짐이나 물건을 트럭·배·기계 등으로 한 곳에서 다른 곳으로 옮길 때 써요. '옮기다'보다 딱딱하고 일하는 느낌이 있어요. 명사 '운반'은 '운반 비용'처럼 써요.

phrases.en: Heavy furniture has a high transport cost.
phrases.nuance_ko: 명사 '운반'에 '비용'이 붙은 짝말로, 물건을 옮기는 데 드는 돈을 말해요.
phrases.nuance_en: A noun pair meaning the money needed to move goods.

phrases.en: Please carry this box up to the second floor.
phrases.nuance_ko: 일하는 사람에게 정중하게 부탁할 때 쓰는 말이에요.
phrases.nuance_en: A polite request, usually to someone doing the work.

phrases.en: My friend and I moved the desk into the room.
phrases.nuance_ko: '운반하다'보다 부드럽고 일상에서 더 자주 쓰는 같은 뜻의 말이에요.
phrases.nuance_en: A softer, more everyday word with a similar meaning.

explain_en: Use it for moving heavy goods from one place to another by truck, ship, or machine. It is stiffer than '옮기다' and feels like work. The noun 운반 appears in '운반 비용' (transport cost).

examples.en: Bedtime is eleven at night.
Don't look at your smartphone before bed.
In the dormitory, lights-out is at twelve.
I drink warm tea before going to bed.

examples.ko: 취침 후에는 방의 불을 꺼 주세요.
examples.en: After bedtime, please turn off the room light.
You get healthier if you go to bed regularly too.

explain: 잠자리에 드는 일을 격식 있게 나타내는 한자어예요. 일상 대화에서는 '자다', '잠자리에 들다'를 쓰고, 기숙사나 군대의 규칙, 안내문에서 '취침 시간'처럼 써요. 반대는 '기상'이에요.

phrases.en: The students go to bed at ten.
phrases.nuance_ko: '취침'에 '하다'를 붙인 동사예요. 기숙사나 군대 같은 곳에서 격식 있게 말할 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: The verb form of 취침, used in formal settings like dormitories or the military.

phrases.example: 우리 기숙사는 취침 시간이 열한 시예요.
phrases.en: Bedtime in our dormitory is eleven o'clock.
phrases.nuance_ko: 자야 하는 시간이에요. 규칙이나 안내문에서 많이 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: The time you must go to bed; common in rules and notices.

phrases.en: I was tired yesterday, so I went to bed early.
phrases.nuance_ko: 취침과 같은 뜻이지만 일상 대화에서 자연스럽게 쓰는 말이에요.
phrases.nuance_en: Same meaning as 취침, but a natural everyday expression.

explain_en: It is a formal Sino-Korean word for going to bed. In daily conversation use '자다' or '잠자리에 들다'; '취침 시간' (bedtime) appears in rules and notices at dormitories and the military. The opposite is '기상' (getting up).
